public_rationale: The claim is restricted to the original concept of AGI as the speaker describes it. Its main part is that AI systems at the time lacked flexible, self-directed competence. The ARC Prize Foundation says ARC-AGI-3 tests agents on exploring novel environments and acquiring goals on the fly (page dated 2026-03-25). Decrypt reported on 2026-03-26 that frontier models scored under 1% at launch: Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.37%, GPT-5.4 0.26%, Claude Opus 4.6 0.25%, Grok-4.20 0%. Humans solved 100% of environments. The concession that systems were powerful and increasingly useful also holds. OfficeChai reported on 2026-02-21 that METR measured Opus 4.6 at a 50% time horizon of about 14.5 hours on software, machine-learning and cybersecurity tasks, on a rising trend. A Nature comment dated 2026-02-02 argued that human-level AI had already arrived. It is argument, not measurement.
limitations: Most of the weight rests on one benchmark, ARC-AGI-3. Its 100% mark means matching human efficiency, not only solving the games.
The ARC-AGI-3 model scores come from a news report, not the foundation's own results page.
The ARC-AGI-3 results came out about five weeks after the post.
The METR estimate has a wide confidence interval (6 to 98 hours), and METR said its task suite was nearly saturated.
'Original concept of AGI' is the speaker's own characterization, and 'flexible, self-directed competence' has no agreed measure.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: in February 2026, frontier AI was useful and improving, but could not flexibly handle unfamiliar situations or set and pursue its own goals the way a human can.

'Current AI systems' means frontier systems available at the post (for example Claude Opus 4.6). The target period is February-March 2026, to include the first independent evaluations of those systems. This choice is flagged.
The 'powerful and increasingly useful' part is a concession, not the main claim; the main claim is the lack of flexible, self-directed competence.
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations from the period show frontier systems failing at tasks that require exploring unfamiliar settings and working out goals without instructions, where humans succeed, while also showing rising capability on narrower tasks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations from the period show frontier systems matching humans at flexible, self-directed tasks in novel environments without human-built help.

evidence.excerpt: Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro led the pack at 0.37%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 came in at 0.26%. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 managed 0.25%, while xAI’s Grok-4.20 scored exactly zero. Humans, meanwhile, solved 100% of environments.
evidence.explanation: Frontier systems scored under 1% where humans scored 100% on tasks requiring self-directed exploration and goal discovery. This is direct evidence of missing flexible, self-directed competence.

evidence.excerpt: challenges AI agents to explore novel environments, acquire goals on the fly, build adaptable world models, and learn continuously.
evidence.explanation: Shows the benchmark measures flexible, self-directed competence of the kind the claim describes.
